findings.claim: The pop-up definition on 'particularistic standards' reads: 'A social position that is fixed at birth, such as gender or family background, regardless of individual effort.'
findings.truth: That is the definition of ascribed status. Particularistic standards are rules applied to one particular child within the family, as the lesson's own glossary and prose say.
findings.evidence: spec 7.2 Parsons ('within the family particularistic standards apply'); the lesson's own glossary entry contradicts the pop-up

findings.claim: 'The mark scheme rewards candidates who present the functionalist view ...'
findings.truth: No mark scheme is cited. A claim about what the board's mark scheme rewards is fabricated, and it breaches the house copyright-distance rule.
findings.evidence: house rule on copyright distancing; the spec carries no mark-scheme wording

findings.claim: KC 4 (fill): 'Marxists argue that the appearance of meritocracy in education serves to ______ class inequality' - options reproduce / legitimise / reinforce / challenge, key = legitimise.
findings.truth: 'Reproduce' and 'reinforce' also complete that sentence, so a student with correct sociology can be marked wrong. The fix is to reword the stem, not to move the key, so it needs an authoring pass rather than a one-field edit.

findings.claim: 'Approximately 7% of pupils in England attend private schools' (repeated as a knowledge-check key).
findings.truth: 7% is the long-standing textbook figure for the UK. DfE school-census data for England puts the independent share nearer 6%. Not worth an edit while 7% is the figure every GCSE textbook uses.
findings.evidence: DfE schools, pupils and their characteristics; ISC census

findings.claim: 'Interactionist response: ... Paul Willis's 1977 study Learning to Labour showed ...' - Willis presented as an interactionist.
findings.truth: Willis wrote from a Marxist perspective. The spec's key-thinker entry opens 'Writing from a Marxist perspective, Paul Willis ...'. A student who calls Willis an interactionist has the attribution wrong.
findings.evidence: spec 7.2 Willis P, Learning to Labour, 1977

findings.truth: The same wrong attribution in the takeaways, which are the part students revise from.

findings.claim: The 3-mark and 12-mark model answers both say 'Willis's interactionist study'.
findings.truth: Willis is a Marxist. The answer key teaches the wrong attribution.

findings.claim: 'Ball argued that "parentocracy" - the rhetoric of parental choice - favours middle-class families'.
findings.truth: 'Parentocracy' was coined by Phillip Brown in 1990, not by Ball. Ball's spec-named contribution is on parental choice and competition between schools.
findings.evidence: spec 3.4.3 and 7.2 (Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz, 1994); Brown, 'The Third Wave: Education and the Ideology of Parentocracy', 1990

findings.claim: 'The specification explicitly requires you to name and describe the mechanisms: material deprivation ..., cultural capital ..., and within-school processes'.
findings.truth: The spec asks students to identify, describe and explain factors affecting achievement including class, gender and ethnicity. It names none of those mechanisms as required.

findings.claim: Flashcard 10: Origins and Destinations was 'conducted in the late 1970s and published in 1980'.
findings.truth: The data came from the 1972 Oxford mobility survey of over 8,000 men born between 1913 and 1952. Only publication was 1980.
findings.evidence: spec 7.2 Halsey, Heath and Ridge, 1980 ('a sample of over 8,000 males born between 1913 and 1952')

findings.claim: Halsey's headline finding appears four times (prose, takeaway, knowledge-check key, model answer) as 'even when pupils of similar measured ability were compared, those from working-class backgrounds were significantly less likely to gain high-level qualifications'.
findings.truth: The spec's account of Origins and Destinations reports chances of staying in education by class origin, not a comparison at matched measured ability: a service-class boy had four times the chance of still being at school at 16, eight times at 17, ten times at 18 and eleven times the chance of reaching university. Options: (a) keep the 'controlling for ability' framing, which several textbooks use but the spec does not; or (b) replace it in all four places with the spec's own figures, which changes a knowledge-check key and its distractors. Recommendation: (b), as a single authoring pass so the key and distractors are rewritten together.
findings.ruling: NOTE: the 'controlling for measured ability' framing is a standard textbook reading of Halsey, Heath and Ridge and is not wrong; the spec's odds figures (4x at 16, 11x university) would be a worthwhile addition in a later authoring pass with the KC rewritten together.

findings.claim: Ball 'investigated the introduction and effects of banding in a fictional comprehensive school (referred to as "Beachside")'.
findings.truth: Beachside was a real south-coast comprehensive given a pseudonym, studied over three years of participant observation. Ball followed two cohorts as the school moved away from banding towards mixed-ability teaching; he did not study the introduction of banding.

findings.claim: 'The spec explicitly names "interactionist" as one of the four perspectives for section 3.4.4.'
findings.truth: The statement is true, but it prints a spec section code in student-facing prose, which the house copyright rule forbids. The teaching point survives without the code.

findings.claim: Under the heading 'Non-participant observation': 'Ball's Beachside Comprehensive research used observation alongside interviews ...'
findings.truth: Beachside was three years of participant observation. Placing it in the non-participant paragraph teaches the wrong method for a named study, in the methods lesson itself.
findings.evidence: spec 7.2 Ball ('three years fieldwork as a participant observer ... this is a participant observation study')

findings.claim: 'Halsey's Origins and Destinations research combined survey data with follow-up interviews ... This mixed-methods approach used triangulation.'
findings.truth: Origins and Destinations was a single large-scale survey of over 8,000 men. It was not a mixed-methods study and is not an example of triangulation. In a methods answer this is a wrong worked example.

findings.claim: Official statistics allow trends to be tracked 'across social class, gender and ethnicity over time - as Halsey's research did'.
findings.truth: Halsey used his own survey rather than official statistics, and the spec notes the research excluded females, so it could show no gender trend at all.

findings.claim: 4-mark model answer: official statistics track achievement 'by class, gender and ethnicity over many years (as Halsey did)'.
findings.truth: The same error in the answer key: Halsey did not use official statistics, and his male-only sample carried no gender data.

findings.claim: Match stem: 'Match each ethical issue to the correct description' - but one of the four items is 'Gatekeeper'.
findings.truth: Gatekeeping is a practical issue of access, not an ethical issue. The pairings are right; only the stem is wrong.
findings.evidence: standard methods vocabulary; the lesson itself puts gatekeepers under 'Practical issues'

summary: Sixteen fixes across five lessons. The two systemic errors are Willis mislabelled as an interactionist (the spec calls him a Marxist) throughout lesson 3, and Halsey's Origins and Destinations misdescribed in lesson 6 as a mixed-methods triangulation study built on official statistics; plus a reversed pop-up definition in lesson 1 and a 'fictional' Beachside in lesson 5. Paper structure, timing and the 1/2/3/4/12 mark ladder are correct throughout, and every knowledge-check key and match order recomputes correctly.
